The simplest thing is to just tell him about energy conservation. Fat is stored energy, so if he's fat he's eating too much. You cannot make energy out of nothing.

This completely bypasses any fatlogic he (or anyone else) can muster because it simply doesn't matter. Even if you have all the fat genes and all the conditions, if you're fat you're eating too much.

What you need is not better studies, but very sharp reasoning about what it means for genetics to play a role in obesity.

Most people will mean: "My metabolism is slow because of my genetics, and I'm fat because my metabolism is slow." This is stupid primarily because of the second part, which is like saying that you overfilled your gas tank because your car is too fuel-efficient. However, I'm confident my fellow shitlords will also have refuted the first part: in magnitude, genetics is a small component in the population's variation of metabolic rates.

However, that's just a particular method by which genetics might play a role in obesity, and a dumb method at that. Heritability is the fraction of variation of a trait within a population that can be explained by genetic variation via any cause. I would be surprised if obesity was less than 30% heritable. Why? Obesity is primarily a side effect of behavior, and damn near any behavioral trait is upwards of 30% heritable. Intelligence: 60-80% heritable. Impulsiveness: 49% (single study). Procrastination: 46% (single study). Self-control. Do you really think that "eating too much" is 0% heritable? No: it's a product of your brain, which is a product of your genes.

This doesn't mean that your weight is genetically determined: it's certainly not 100% heritable. It's also important to realize that using partial heritability of something as an excuse to make no effort is unbelievably fucking stupid fatalism. You don't know for sure that your brain lacks the discipline to do something, unless you don't even try, in which case it definitely does. It would be like saying that there's no point in trying to quit drinking because alcoholism is (no doubt) partially heritable.

So, the fact remains that your genes affect your brain, which affects your behavior, which affects your weight, and that's all that OP's NIH study is saying. I understand that some people hate any notion of genes affecting behavior, but that's a separate debate: OP's NIH study does not look like fattie bullshit to me. Rather, it comes across slightly shitlordy:

"Recent progress in the elucidation of polygenic predisposition to obesity also points to a key role of the central nervous system in body weight regulation [17]."

Translation: Your brain makes you fat.

"The genetic dissection of monogenic and polygenic forms of obesity delineate it as an inherited disorder of central regulation of food intake [16]."

Translation: Obesity is an inherited disorder where your brain fails to control how much you eat.

"This is in line with the fact that food intake-related parameters are heritable [29] and are strongly correlated to body mass index [30]."

Translation: Eating behavior is heritable, and eating behavior strongly affects your weight.

The study isn't all shitlord fun and games. For example, genetic factors influencing hunger may be involved, which is less perfect than a pure issue of discipline being heritable. And it talks about the possibility of using genes to decide who gets bariatric surgery. I guess I may be giving the study a light touch because I agree that genes affect behavior.

Nonetheless, it's still reality that your weight is mostly controlled by your behavior and your behavior is significantly influenced by your genes. If your friend's brain leads him to take that reality and decide that he can't control his behavior, perhaps his partially-inherited intelligence was not up to snuff.

TL;DR of my post: Yes, you were short-changed by your genes, fatty. Not because of your metabolism, dummy, but because they didn't give you a brain with the intelligence to realize that you should stop eating so much and the self-control to execute your decision.
